extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers studying U.S. constitutional law and government
extracted.subtask_short: explaining judicial review and federal courts
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter explaining the role, powers, and limits of the Federal courts in the U.S. constitutional system, including judicial review, hierarchy of laws, separation of powers, and practical procedural duties. Emphasizes principles that determine when statutes or subordinate acts are valid or void and which tribunals must decide those questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure of Federal courts prescribed by Congress subject to Constitutional rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure of the Federal courts is prescribed by Congress, but subject to a few constitutional rules (for example, preservation of the right of trial by jury in criminal cases and in suits at common law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress may set federal procedure generally, but cannot override specific constitutional procedural guarantees; e.g., Congress could not fuse law and equity into one procedure where the Constitution requires distinct methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of law in Federal courts (federal law prevails; otherwise apply state law)
rubrics_metrics.description: When federal law is applicable it prevails against any State law; when Federal law does not apply (or only secondarily), the court must determine what law ought to govern the case and apply that State's law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In diversity or other cases where state law governs, federal courts apply the particular State's constitution, statutes, and common law (including civil law in Louisiana) and should treat state court decisions as the highest authority on that State's law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to State courts on State law
rubrics_metrics.description: In administering the law of any State the Federal courts ought to follow the decisions of the State courts, treating those decisions as the highest authority on the law of the particular State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts may even overrule their own prior determinations on a point of State law to align with the view of the highest court of the State; conversely, State courts follow Federal decisions on Federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties and chain of command for Federal judicial officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Federal court has attached officers such as the United States marshal (to carry out writs, judgments, arrests, levies, custody arrangements) and the United States district attorney (to institute proceedings against violators of Federal laws or evaders of Federal obligations), both under the Attorney-General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marshals may call on citizens for assistance and, if resisted, may seek Federal troops; where State gaols exist, marshals deliver prisoners to State gaolers; otherwise they arrange custody themselves. These officials form a nationwide network independent of State officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that Federal law applicability entitles suitor to Federal determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Federal law is applicable, Federal law must prevail, and any suitor who contends that Federal law is applicable is entitled to have that point determined by a Federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule helps prevent conflicts and ensures parties can obtain a federal forum to assert the applicability of federal law; the abundance of precedents and legal expertise aids resolution of jurisdiction and applicability questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of functions between legislature and judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature makes the law; the judiciary investigates facts and applies the law to particular cases. Nevertheless, there are debatable points where legislative and judicial functions touch (e.g., impeachment trials, disputed parliamentary elections, special/local bills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the lines between functions can be blurred in practice, the judiciary's essential role is interpretation and application of law; comparative practices (England vs. U.S.) influence which functions are entrusted to courts vs. legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on legislature exercising judicial power (no bills of attainder)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature is forbidden to exercise the powers of a criminal court by passing acts of attainder or of pains and penalties; such measures are not permissible in the U.S. constitutional system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This safeguard secures individual rights against legislative caprice and is one respect in which the American system departs from older English practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of subordinate bodies' rules depends on scope of conferred authority (ultra vires doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts or rules made by subordinate bodies (or executive officers) have the force of law only when made within the scope of the authority conferred; if they transcend that power they are null and void and not law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to agency law: bye-laws of companies or municipal corporations exceeding statutory powers bind nobody; examples include railway bye-laws imposing penalties beyond statutory limits or municipal bye-laws that fail to comply with statutory conditions. Courts, not the subordinate body, decide validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen right to resist orders beyond a magistrate's legal power
rubrics_metrics.description: A citizen is justified in disobeying the orders of a magistrate if those orders are correctly believed to be in excess of the magistrate's legal power, because such orders are not lawful commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In free countries executive power is strictly limited by law; the ordinary courts will protect individuals who resist unlawful officer actions (e.g., acquit them if prosecuted or grant civil judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review: courts determine constitutionality of statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a congressional statute transgresses the Constitution must be determined by the courts (National/Federal courts), not by Congress or the President, because interpretation of laws belongs to courts and Congress/President are interested parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination involves setting the statute alongside the Constitution to see if purposes or clauses conflict; often this requires trained lawyers and consideration of precedent. Only impartial courts can reliably vindicate constitutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of law in the American system
rubrics_metrics.description: American laws have four degrees of authority: (I) The Federal Constitution; (II) Federal statutes; (III) State constitutions; (IV) State statutes. Treaties have the same authority as Federal statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Constitution prevails against all others; Federal statutes, if made pursuant to the Constitution, prevail against state constitutions and statutes; if Federal statutes exceed constitutional powers they are invalid to that extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of conflicts between laws of different authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When a conflict exists between laws of different degrees of authority (e.g., Federal vs. State), the court's role is to declare that a conflict exists and thereby indicate the inferiority (and invalidity) of the weaker law; the court decides only the case before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaration of unconstitutionality is not a repeal of a statute; another litigant may bring a fresh case raising the same question. In practice, courts often settle such issues; the public and profession generally accept the court's authoritative view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Federal courts because State courts might be partial
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts were established co-extensive with national authority because State courts, as offspring of State governments, might naturally tend to uphold State laws against the Federal Constitution or statutes; Federal courts provide an impartial forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context: colonial decisions and early State cases show courts cancelling legislative acts that exceeded charters or constitutions; Federal courts continue that role at the national level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive process: comparison of statute purpose and constitutional provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether a statute is within constitutional power requires comparing the statute's purpose with the purposes mentioned or implied in the Constitution and checking whether it contains anything violating constitutional clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes straightforward, often difficult; requires legal subtlety and knowledge of precedent. The legislature makes general rules relying on courts to interpret and apply them to specific circumstances.
